articleTitle: Case Studies: New Options for Power Factor Correction
abstract: Utilities across the United States are increasingly using underground cable for both new construction and replacement of overhead facilities. The properties of the cable have a capacitive effect, which tends to raise voltage during light loading conditions and create leading power factor. Poor power factor can reduce the usable capacity of equipment, and transmission providers are increasingly pressuring distribution utilities to improve the power factor of their facilities. Longer, lightly used underground feeders, large motors, and other factors inherent to an electric distribution system can create voltage instability and other power quality issues which can compound the problem.Large motors also create an adverse effect on distribution systems, creating flicker and poor voltage conditions for other consumers sharing the same circuit. Combined with poor power factor, power quality issues are compounded.Historically, utilities have found it necessary to correct lagging power factor through the application of shunt capacitors. In recent years, trends have moved toward leading power factor, and along with it, the need to consider new options for power factor correction. The focus of this document is to highlight case studies of three rural electric cooperatives: provide an overview of their power factor issues, options that were considered, and final implementation.

articleTitle: Benefit of Fast Reactive Power Response from Inverters in Weak Distribution Systems
abstract: Electric power systems worldwide tend to become inverter-dominated. We witness an increasing integration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) in both transmission and distribution systems along with a decline in the share of synchronous generators. Unlike synchronous machines, today's IBRs have relatively small contribution to system strength, which can be quantified by the reduced short circuit level in an IBR dominated grid. As a result, the short circuit ratio at a distribution substation may decrease, which may expose the distribution connected IBRs to weak grid operating conditions. This paper investigates the potential stability challenges that may occur in such conditions. A potential instability issue with the present-day inverter controls is identified and the mitigation effect of two alternative control methods is demonstrated. Fast reactive power response, which is a common feature of the two alternative methods, is discussed to be a potential performance requirement to mitigate the instability.

articleTitle: Revit 3D Modeling Optimizes Substation Design
abstract: Designing substations and generating drawing packages using 2D software is a mainstay in the power industry. However, the engineering services market is pushing companies to explore options for 3D modeling software to remain competitive. 3D design has the possibility to drive a more integrated process and eliminate inefficiencies that arise during manual 2D drafting. This method could streamline design changes and communication across disciplines, cut down on drafting workload, and change how engineers have approach even boilerplate designs for substations.This paper reviews a 3D substation pilot project developed using Revit software, a software widely used in architecture that was adapted for engineering purposes. Instead of creating a drawing package, this software focuses on creating a design from which individual components can be broken out. The benefits, lessons learned, and potential industry-wide impact of adopting 3D software for substation design will be further explored in this paper.

articleTitle: Novel RVSS Motor Control Method to Limit PCC Voltage Sag During Ramp Start
abstract: This paper describes a novel reduced voltage soft starter motor control method to limit point of common coupling sag during a ramp start to a certain programmed threshold level. As background information, an across the line full voltage start of an induction motor results in full locked rotor current until the shaft comes up to speed. Whereas a RVSS is employed to electronically limit the current applied to the motor to a fraction of the locked rotor value which has many benefits that will be listed in the presentation. In this paper a real-time hardware in the loop computer simulation, and medium voltage actual laboratory experiments, are used to sweep varying source impedances to compare multiple soft-starter control methods to the novel sag controlled sag method. The soft starter sag control method may be appreciated in weak source implementations such as rural installations and additionally in process control where motor starting sequences and loading at the time of ramp start can be dynamic.

articleTitle: Leveraging Technology for Automation and NERC Compliance
abstract: This paper presents a summary and analysis for a Multi-vendor Device Management system, focusing on automated Event and Fault File collection and Remote Engineering Access, while implementing cyber-security and compliance management for a utility in North America. An investigation into technologies for improving automated fault and event file collection with an effort to reduce the time required for service restoration to customers was the starting point for this project. There was also a requirement to secure their system with regards to the North America Reliability Corporation (NERC) Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) standards. This report is intended for anyone considering the implementation of a Multi-vendor Device Management system and cyber-security strategy securing substation devices.

articleTitle: The Grounded Wye-Delta Transformer with a Zig-Zag Transformer
abstract: A most common use of a zig-zag transformer connection is to provide a grounding source for a three-wire delta connected distribution line. When a ground fault occurs on a delta line since there is no ground return path it is impossible to detect that the fault has occurred. In such cases a zig- zag transformer can be connected at the source to provide a path for the ground current to flow back to the source. This paper describes the basic zig-zag transformer and develops a general model that includes the grounded wye-delta bank and the zig-zag transformer. Results of power-flow and short circuit analyses are included using a new test feeder that is like the IEEE Four Node Test Feeder.

articleTitle: Re-Engineering Overhead Line Design
abstract: This document presents foundational concepts for design and construction of overhead utility lines to ensure NESC compliance as it relates to loading and clearances.

articleTitle: Enhancing distribution system resiliency using grid-forming fuel cell inverter
abstract: Legacy inverters interfacing distributed energy re-sources are traditionally grid-following (GFL) in nature. GFL assets typically follow real power and reactive power set points. Recently, inverters with grid-forming (GFM) capability are gaining attention because GFM assets can increase the resiliency of the distribution system under stressed conditions. These GFM inverters can use photovoltaics, batteries, or fuel cells as their energy source. In this paper, we present information on inverters interfacing fuel cell assets, specifically with GFM capability. By introducing a fuel cell-powered GFM coupled with hydrogen production and storage, the GFM can continuously provide GFM activities during periods of low renewable resource availability and/or during power outages exceeding typical electric battery duration. Finally, we present information on the need for updates to interconnection and interoperability standards that can be leveraged by utilities for including fuel cell inverters in their asset mixes.

articleTitle: Adaptive Protective Relay Settings – A Vision to the Future
abstract: Adaptive relaying utilizes the continuously changing status of the power system as the basis for online adjustment of the power system relay settings. Fundamentally they are protection schemes that adjust settings and/or logic of operations based on the prevailing conditions of the system. These adjustments can include, but are not limited to, the logging of data for post-mortem analysis, communication throughout the system, as well as changing relay parameters. Adaptive relaying considers the fact that the status of a power system can change. These include system configuration changes, load effect, cold load pickup, end-of-line protection, transformer protection, and automatic reclosing. In this research, the author focus on the need for a secure, selective, and reliable system for adaptive overcurrent protection in T&D and Distributed Energy Systems. Various types of adaptive methods are presented and explained along with some pros and cons of each.

articleTitle: Model-Based Interface Design for Smart Field-Device Integration
abstract: Operational complexity is ever-increasing for electric utilities that face challenges including integration of DERs, customer expectation of energy choices, the proliferation of non-utility-owned resources, new business models with energy service providers, and new technology with IT/OT convergence. To maintain and improve the quality of operations, planning, and decision-making in general, utilities need to manage and navigate the complexity. Managing complexity requires a modular, scalable, and flexible solution. Connecting large amounts of DERs and introducing new services requires increased grid control and evolving applications. In this paper, we show an approach utilizing model-based standardized interfaces that simplifies integration and deployment of new algorithms and smart field devices for interoperability across legacy or new systems. A modular design is presented for a reference implementation of widely used DNP3 and IEEE 2030.5 interfaces within an open-source, standards-based data integration platform for integration of smart field devices with independently developed, best-of-breed applications.

articleTitle: Modeling Distributed Energy Resources for Analyzing Distribution Systems with High Renewable Penetration
abstract: Increasing levels of inverter-based distributed energy resources (IBDERs) impact the legacy overcurrent distribution protection systems. The fault current injections of IBDERs are limited to between 1.25–2.25 p.u. of the rated current. The combination of the limited fault current and varying system load makes it increasingly difficult to reliably set the overcurrent protection. To address this challenge, researchers are proposing adaptive overcurrent protection mechanisms that can adapt to changing system conditions. Accurate modeling of IBDERs is required to develop reliable protection schemes. This paper presents a photovoltaics-based IBDER model in OpenDSS for adaptive overcurrent protection. The paper presents the validation of the proposed IBDER model against a detailed model in electromagnetic transient programs. Protection analysis of the Electric Power Research Institute J1 feeder with the proposed IBDER model is also presented.

articleTitle: Analysis of Battery Energy Storage with Distribution Electric Grid Connected Solar Projects
abstract: In many parts of the United States, solar-plus-storage projects are fast replacing retiring coal-based thermal power plants while strongly competing against natural gas combined cycle turbines and/or peaker plants. Today, the electrochemical energy storage market dominated by the Lithium-ion battery chemistries (mainly by Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt Oxide (Li-NMC) and Lithium Ferrous Phosphate (LFP)) is fast becoming a vital component of the distribution electric grid due to a multitude of applications, and declining capital costs. Electrochemical battery energy storage is being perceived as the missing piece in the puzzle of integration of intermittent renewables to the electric grid. This research is an analysis conducted on two operating solar-plus-storage projects interconnected to two rural electric distribution utility substations. The analysis evaluates the summer and winter demand reduction due to solar-plus-storage projects at the distribution grid level while quantifying the economic value. This research also discusses the project design approaches and other benefits of solar-plus-storage projects such as energy arbitrage, frequency and voltage support, active demand response, backup power, distribution system upgrade deferrals etc.

articleTitle: Integrating Distributed Devices onto Rural Circuits
abstract: Utilities typically prioritize the satisfaction of their customers. Their customers expect the highest levels of reliability as many day-to-day activities involve loads requiring a constant energy supply. In urban areas, to ensure this reliability factor, many utilities use networked systems so there are several paths for generation to reach a customer in the event of an outage. These systems inherently build redundancy through their configuration and switching abilities. In rural areas, however, lower population densities and power system branches cause the reliability techniques used in urban areas to become less practical. Consequently, customers in rural areas experience more outages and longer outage times due to the distance between customers. Not only are longer lines more vulnerable to environmental hazards such as trees, weather, and cars, but outages also affect all downstream customers who need to wait for repair trucks to get dispatched to rural areas, increasing outage times.Current research focuses on the integration of distributed generation, mostly with solar, to support rural circuits. This paper will explore the impact of integrating distributed storage in rural systems at the edge of the grid. We will use models to evaluate how these feeders accommodate new devices and how they impact the reliability of the circuit. In addition, different levels of penetration are compared to anticipate the effect of future devices, such as electric vehicles, which have similar behavior and are becoming more popular. This exploration can help predict the threshold for electric vehicles before utilities need to investigate and make upgrades.

articleTitle: Case Study of a Solar-plus-storage Hybrid Generation Plant for Georgia’s Electric Cooperatives
abstract: Grid-connected energy storage offers multiple advantages to power grid operators who strive to optimize the use of renewable generation assets and solve operational issues that occur with higher renewable penetration. Due to the declining cost of battery cell technologies, battery energy storage systems (BESSs) are being deployed across the country. Electric Membership Cooperatives (EMCs) in Georgia are interested in BESS capabilities as distributed energy resources and as a means to complement utility-scale solar generation as they strive to meet the demands of a transitioning energy landscape. As a research and development project, Green Power EMC, the not-for-profit electric cooperative that secures renewable energy resources for 38 Georgia EMCs, has commissioned and now operates a 250 kW/548 kWh BESS paired with a 1 MW solar generation facility located on one of their member cooperative’s feeder near an industrial load. Proving the methods for design, testing, control, and maintenance at a scaled-down site is necessary before investment of grid-impactful storage systems is required to facilitate higher levels of intermittent renewable resources at the transmission and distribution level. A novel plant controller was implemented to demonstrate the following modes of operation: peak demand reduction, retail rate reduction, and solar intermittency control. Despite a distribution interconnection, the plant is operated with standard transmission equipment with connection to the statewide SCADA system for real-time data of operating parameters and battery diagnostics. The paper describes the present progress and lessons learned from this project thus-far with analysis of the plant’s operational data.
